Breast augmentation (breast implants) information published by healthdirect — what the procedure involves, benefits and considerations, preparation, recovery, complications, alternatives and Australian support resources, extracted and linked to the original page.

This library collects healthdirect’s public patient information on breast augmentation (breast implants) and the Australian resources it links to. Every entry links to the original page on healthdirect.gov.au or to the Australian body named in the entry, so the wording, review dates and any subsequent updates can be checked at source.

What this library does and does not mean

healthdirect is a free Australian Government health information service, not a regulator or a clinic. Its pages describe breast augmentation as it is practised and paid for in Australia, what the operation involves and what can go wrong. Nothing here is a recommendation to have a procedure, and healthdirect does not endorse any clinic, surgeon or treatment package.

Summaries and key points are condensed from the healthdirect page for readability. They are not a substitute for the original document, which was last reviewed in November 2025 and may have been updated since this library was compiled on 2026-10-20. Always read the current version on healthdirect.gov.au and discuss it with a qualified clinician.

Coverage

What the healthdirect information covers

The library is grouped into five areas, from what the procedure is through to recovery, risks and alternatives.

The procedure

What breast augmentation is, how implants are placed, anaesthetic, fat grafting and the TGA status of breast implant products in Australia.

Decisions and consent

Benefits people expect, the points healthdirect says to weigh up, and the questions to ask before surgery.

Preparation and cost

Getting fit, quitting smoking, GP referral, checking your surgeon on AHPRA and RACS, Medicare and the components of cost.

Recovery

Time off work, exercise limits, drains and dressings, and the symptoms that mean calling your surgeon or going to hospital.

Complications

Bleeding, infection, sensation changes, rupture, and the rarer serious risks including clots and implant-associated cancer.

Alternatives and support

Counselling, padded bras and non-implant surgery, plus Australian resources and the 24/7 healthdirect helpline.

What breast augmentation is

How healthdirect describes the procedure itself, why people choose it, and the points it says to weigh up before deciding.

What is breast augmentation?

Procedure page section · Reviewed November 2025

healthdirect defines breast augmentation as a form of cosmetic surgery that enlarges the breasts, also called breast enlargement or breast reconstruction. Implants sit either under the breast or under the chest muscle and consist of a silicone shell filled with saline (salty water) or silicone gel. Some surgeons also offer fat grafting, moving fat from another part of the body into the breast. The page notes that reconstruction after mastectomy is a separate topic, and that a Therapeutic Goods Administration (TGA) review led to some breast implants being withdrawn from the Australian market or given conditions on their use.

  • Breast augmentation is cosmetic surgery to make the breasts larger; it is also referred to as breast enlargement.
  • Implants are placed under the breast or beneath the chest muscle and are made of a silicone shell filled with saline or silicone gel.
  • Some cosmetic surgeons offer fat grafting, transferring fat from areas such as the buttocks into the breasts.
  • Reconstruction after a mastectomy uses implants or tissue for a different purpose; that is separate from cosmetic augmentation.
  • After a TGA review, some breast implant products have been removed from the Australian market or had conditions placed on them.

Read the original on healthdirect.gov.au →

What are the benefits of breast augmentation?

Procedure page section · Reviewed November 2025

healthdirect states that people consider breast augmentation for many reasons, most commonly a desire to feel more physically attractive or more comfortable with themselves. The page frames the benefit in terms of how the person hopes to feel rather than promising any particular result.

  • Reasons people give include wanting to feel more physically attractive or better about themselves.
  • healthdirect does not guarantee an outcome; expectations should be discussed with a surgeon.

Read the original on healthdirect.gov.au →

What should I consider before choosing to have breast augmentation?

Procedure page section · Reviewed November 2025

healthdirect acknowledges social pressure around body shape and asks readers to weigh several points before deciding: implants are not lifelong and usually need replacing after 10 to 15 years; cancer has very rarely arisen in the fluid and scar tissue around an implant; some people are unhappy with how their breasts look afterwards; implants can make breast cancer harder to detect during screening; and breastfeeding may be affected.

  • Implants do not last for life and usually need replacing after 10 to 15 years.
  • There have been rare cases of cancer developing in the fluid and scar tissue around an implant.
  • Some people find the result does not look the way they hoped.
  • Implants can make it harder to detect breast cancer during screening checks.
  • The ability to breastfeed may change after surgery.
  • Body image and social pressure are worth examining before deciding, and counselling is an option.

Read the original on healthdirect.gov.au →

Current status of breast implant products in Australia

Regulator callout on the healthdirect page · Reviewed November 2025

The healthdirect page carries a callout about a Therapeutic Goods Administration (TGA) review after which some breast implants were removed from the Australian market or had conditions placed on them, and links to the TGA's current status page for the details.

  • The TGA reviewed breast implant products and some were withdrawn from the Australian market or given conditions of use.
  • The TGA website publishes the current status of breast implant products in Australia.
  • The TGA also publishes information on breast implants and anaplastic large cell lymphoma (BIA-ALCL).

The procedure and preparation

Anaesthetic and implant placement, how to prepare for surgery, choosing a surgeon through AHPRA and RACS, what Medicare covers, and the questions healthdirect suggests asking before surgery.

What does a breast augmentation procedure involve?

Procedure page section · Reviewed November 2025

The procedure is normally done under general anaesthetic so the patient sleeps throughout. The surgeon cuts alongside the breast and positions the implant either between the breast tissue and the muscle, or behind the large chest muscle under the breast; the surgeon decides which method suits the patient. Different surgical techniques are available, and the method chosen can affect recovery time.

  • General anaesthetic is usually required, so you are asleep during the operation.
  • The surgeon makes a cut alongside the breast.
  • The implant is placed either between the breast tissue and the muscle, or behind the chest muscle.
  • The surgeon chooses the method, and the technique used can affect how long recovery takes.

Read the original on healthdirect.gov.au →

How can I prepare for a breast augmentation?

Procedure page section · Reviewed November 2025

healthdirect advises gathering as much information as possible and preparing by getting physically fit, reaching a healthy weight, trying to stop smoking, asking about medication changes, disclosing health conditions and allergies, and confirming whether you will stay overnight. On choosing a surgeon, it says to pick someone you feel comfortable with who will be honest about benefits and risks, notes that a GP must refer cosmetic surgery patients to their surgeon, and points to the AHPRA register where you can confirm the surgeon is a Fellow of the Royal Australasian College of Surgeons (RACS) and check for serious disciplinary action. On cost, Medicare generally does not cover cosmetic surgery, private health insurance should be checked, and fees typically include the surgeon, anaesthetist, clinic or hospital, the implants, and medication, dressings and support garments. The page lists questions to ask about implant type, sensation, nipple position and appearance, bruising and pain, plus long-term questions about implant lifespan, breastfeeding, rupture, the likelihood of further operations and the cost of any repeat surgery.

  • Prepare by getting physically fit, maintaining a healthy weight and trying to quit smoking.
  • Ask whether any medications need to change, tell the surgeon about health conditions and allergies, and confirm whether you will stay overnight or go home.
  • Choose a surgeon you feel comfortable with who will discuss benefits and risks honestly.
  • A GP needs to make the referral to the surgeon you choose for cosmetic surgery.
  • Check the AHPRA register to confirm your surgeon is a Fellow of the Royal Australasian College of Surgeons (RACS) and to see whether serious disciplinary action has been taken.
  • Medicare generally does not cover cosmetic surgery; check your private health policy for any cover.
  • Costs usually include surgeon and anaesthetist fees, clinic or hospital fees, the implants, and medication, dressings and support garments.
  • Ask what implant type is recommended and why, whether sensation will change, how the nipples will be affected, and what bruising, swelling and pain to expect.
  • Ask how long implants last, whether you will be able to breastfeed, how many of the surgeon's patients have had a ruptured or failed implant, how likely further operations are, and whether extra surgery would cost more.

Read the original on healthdirect.gov.au →

Recovery and warning signs

What to expect after surgery, the support typically needed while healing, and the symptoms that mean you should contact your surgeon or go to hospital.

How soon will I recover?

Procedure page section · Reviewed November 2025

Recovery depends on your health before surgery and your surgeon's advice; you may be asked to take a week off work and avoid moderate exercise for around five weeks. Tubes draining fluid, dressings and a compression bandage are common, along with pain and discomfort from swelling and bruising. Pain relief, extra support garments, time off work, help at home and a follow-up visit are often needed. healthdirect says to contact your surgeon or go to a hospital emergency department if you develop fever, severe pain, nausea or vomiting during recovery.

  • Recovery varies with your pre-surgery health and your surgeon's advice.
  • You may be asked to take about a week off work and avoid moderate exercise for around five weeks.
  • Drain tubes, dressings and a compression bandage may be used, and pain, swelling and bruising are normal early on.
  • You may need pain relief, support garments for a few weeks, time off work, help with daily tasks and a follow-up appointment.
  • Fever, severe pain, nausea or vomiting during recovery means you should contact your surgeon or go to a hospital emergency department.

Read the original on healthdirect.gov.au →

When should I see my doctor?

Procedure page section · Reviewed November 2025

healthdirect lists the symptoms that mean contacting your surgeon straight away after surgery: a temperature above 38°C or chills; nausea, vomiting, shortness of breath or diarrhoea; heavy bleeding from the wound; bleeding or fluid leakage that starts more than a day after surgery; redness around the implant that is worsening or spreading; and increasing pain or tenderness. In an emergency, go to hospital or call triple zero (000).

  • Contact your surgeon straight away for a temperature over 38°C or chills.
  • Nausea, vomiting, shortness of breath or diarrhoea after surgery need urgent review.
  • Heavy bleeding from the wound, or bleeding or fluid leakage starting more than one day after surgery, needs urgent review.
  • Redness around the implant that worsens or spreads, and increasing pain or tenderness, should be reported.
  • Fever, vomiting or heavy bleeding also warrants going to your nearest hospital.

Read the original on healthdirect.gov.au →

Complications and risks

The possible problems healthdirect lists after breast implant surgery, from bleeding and infection to rarer serious risks.

What complications can happen?

Procedure page section · Reviewed November 2025

Like any operation, breast implant surgery carries risks that should be discussed in detail with a surgeon. healthdirect lists bleeding or a haematoma, infection, changed sensation or numbness in the breast skin or nipple, swelling or a fluid collection, injury to surrounding tissue and implant rupture. Rarer serious risks include an allergic reaction to the anaesthetic, blood clots in the legs that can travel to the lungs, and breast implant-associated cancer — implants previously linked with cancer are no longer available. Severe chest pain or trouble breathing means calling triple zero (000) for an ambulance.

  • Possible problems include bleeding or a haematoma, infection, altered sensation or numbness, swelling or fluid collections, injury to nearby tissue and implant rupture.
  • Rarer serious risks include allergic reaction to the anaesthetic and blood clots in the legs that can travel to the lungs.
  • Breast implant-associated cancer is listed as a rare serious risk; implants linked with cancer in the past are no longer available.
  • Risks should be discussed in detail with your surgeon before you consent.
  • Trouble breathing or severe chest pain requires calling triple zero (000) for an ambulance.

Read the original on healthdirect.gov.au →

Alternatives and Australian resources

Options other than implants, plus the Australian organisations, fact sheets and helplines healthdirect points readers to.

Are there alternatives to breast augmentation?

Procedure page section · Reviewed November 2025

healthdirect states that breast augmentation may not be right for everyone and lists counselling to help with accepting your body shape, wearing a padded bra, and other types of surgery that do not involve implants as alternatives.

  • Counselling to help you accept your body shape is offered as an alternative.
  • Wearing a padded bra is a non-surgical alternative.
  • Other surgery that does not use implants may also be an option.

Read the original on healthdirect.gov.au →

Resources and support

Procedure page section · Reviewed November 2025

healthdirect recommends discussing the decision with your doctor first and links to the Australian Society of Plastic Surgeons, the Agency for Clinical Innovation breast implant safety patient information sheet, an Australian Government fact sheet on cosmetic surgery, and the TGA guide to the five questions to ask before getting a medical implant (available in community languages). It also gives the healthdirect helpline on 1800 022 222 (NURSE-ON-CALL in Victoria), staffed by registered nurses 24 hours a day, seven days a week.

  • Discuss the decision with your doctor before going further.
  • The Australian Society of Plastic Surgeons and the Agency for Clinical Innovation publish patient information on breast implants.
  • The Australian Government has a cosmetic surgery fact sheet, and the TGA publishes a guide to questions to ask before a medical implant.
  • The healthdirect helpline (1800 022 222, NURSE-ON-CALL in Victoria) is staffed by registered nurses 24/7.

Read the original on healthdirect.gov.au →

Jurisdiction and copyright

healthdirect pages describe practice, costs and regulation in Australia. Medicare, private insurance, GP referral rules, AHPRA registration and TGA device decisions are Australian arrangements; standards differ between countries and local rules still apply wherever a procedure is performed.

Summaries and facts on this page are paraphrased from healthdirect patient information published by the Australian Government. This library stores only summaries, extracted facts and links; refer to healthdirect’s content policy for the original terms.

For UK patient information, see the NHS information library. For US regulator guidance, see the FDA information library. For professional-society patient information on breast augmentation, see the ASPS information library. For published research, see the PMC research library.
